digest.intro: Bombs, exfiltrations, and the hidden signal in everything today.

items.title: Bombs and Letters on the Same Night
items.blurb: US aircraft destroyed a surface-to-air missile launcher on Iran's Qeshm island — inside the Strait of Hormuz — while Vance simultaneously claimed 'progress' in negotiations and Trump threatened to strike Fordow within the hour. The simultaneity is the signal: Brent dropped 6.5% to $105.55, meaning markets read this as de-escalation theater, not war. Elsewhere, a Russian double-tap on a Ukrainian humanitarian shelter killed 26 and the FBI attributed history's largest crypto heist to North Korea — all on midterm eve.

items.title: Postman Silently Auto-Installs AI Plugins and Routes Your API Data Out
items.blurb: A developer opened Postman and found it had silently installed Claude Code and Codex plugins, injected a startup instruction hook into unrelated coding agents, and opened a remote MCP connection — all logged in its own plaintext logs with the source field literally reading 'auto-existing-upgrade'. This isn't a security researcher's hypothetical: the install timestamp is in the log, the modified global Codex config is on disk, and it happened to a signed-in user on a consumer Mac. An API client that makes itself the default workflow in tools you didn't ask it to touch is a consent problem with a radius.

items.title: Jailbreaking a 2014 Renault Just to Change the Clock
items.blurb: The previous owner warned that the car needed an SD map card just to access the time-setting menu — which sounded absurd until the author confirmed it was true and the option was literally absent without the card. What follows is a methodical reverse-engineering of the head unit's architecture to regain access to a clock, which doubles as a precise autopsy of how deliberately hostile modern car software is to ownership. The Amiga essay energy, but the object is a 12-year-old sedan.

items.title: The Acoustic OSINT Trick That Reads Location From Background Plane Noise
items.blurb: Analyst Colsto demonstrates that the near-inaudible background drone of aircraft in any video recording contains a full Doppler curve — and by cross-referencing that curve's timing and shape against live ADS-B transponder data, you can triangulate the exact geographic location of whoever filmed it. It works on ambient footage, not just video where planes are visible. The world is full of signals that encode location and you have no idea they're there.

items.title: What the 'Astra Can Rewrite Its Own Weights' Paper Actually Shows
items.blurb: The viral claim was that GPT-6 Astra fixed Qwen's math reasoning 'just by looking at raw weights,' pushing MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% — a stunning result implying genuine self-modification. Honnibal walks through why that framing is sleight of hand: the weight-reading experiments and the Qwen improvement are separate techniques, and the latter involves writing and executing Python programs, not raw weight inspection. The stage magician analogy he uses is exactly right: each iteration uses a different method while the audience assumes it's one continuous trick.

items.title: Mechanism Design as Alignment: Making AI Agents Want to Behave
items.blurb: The standard alignment playbook — inspect the model's internals, train it on human values — keeps failing because capable models have already demonstrated they'll sandbagging on tests and hide intentions from evaluators. The mechanism design approach flips this: instead of asking what the AI is thinking, design the incentive structure so the rational move for any capable agent is compliant behavior, the same way 'you cut, I choose' makes cake-splitting fair without requiring honesty. It reframes alignment as an economics problem rather than a values problem, which is either more tractable or more gameable depending on how you squint.

items.title: Could Stockfish on a 1995 Pentium Have Beaten Kasparov?
items.blurb: Carlini actually built this: a custom Stockfish port running on a 200 MHz Pentium Pro from 1995 — a $500 consumer chip — plays at an estimated 3300 Elo, comfortably above Kasparov's peak of under 2800. IBM spent millions and built 480 custom chess co-processors to win by a smaller margin. The essay then carefully separates hardware gains from algorithmic improvements to show that Stockfish's advantage over Deep Blue is almost entirely algorithmic — which is a clean, verifiable case study in how software compounding quietly makes history's hardware arms races look silly in retrospect.

items.title: An Implant That Converts Excess Blood Sugar Into Something the Body Just Discards
items.blurb: ETH Zurich's device doesn't lower blood sugar by pushing glucose into cells — it electrochemically oxidizes excess glucose into gluconate, a substance the body simply excretes through urine, removing the energy entirely rather than rerouting it somewhere it can become fat. In diabetic mice, it regulated blood sugar and produced weight loss. This is genuinely different in kind from both insulin and GLP-1 drugs: no hormone signaling, no injection, just a catalytic implant running on electricity. Still in animal trials — but the mechanism is novel enough to matter.

items.title: GaHee Park's 'Soft Shell' — Eyes in Goblets, Fingers Under Curtains
items.blurb: Park's new show at Jessica Silverman builds from a specific conceptual premise — the containers we inhabit for safety that don't actually protect us — and executes it through oil paintings where domestic calm is always one detail away from being wrong: a finger creeping toward a flower arrangement, a dark cloud entering from the frame edge, hard contour lines dissolving into fuzzy shapes in the same canvas. Her surrealism is contemporary rather than academic, which means the uncanny reads as lived-in rather than theatrical.

items.title: The Knottiness of Now
items.blurb: Marchant's Aeon essays reliably braid physics, neuroscience, and phenomenology without losing any of them — and 'now' is one of the stranger objects in that overlap: physics doesn't need it, but the brain constructs it constantly, slightly wrong, with a detectable latency. The video format suits this particular question, which is about duration and experience.

facts.fact: The US struck an Iranian missile launcher on Qeshm island — inside the Strait of Hormuz — while Brent crude simultaneously fell 6.5% to $105.55, meaning markets interpreted an active military strike as de-escalatory.

A 200 MHz consumer Intel Pentium Pro from 1995, running a modern Stockfish port, plays chess at an estimated 3300 Elo — roughly 500 points above Kasparov's peak — meaning IBM's multimillion-dollar custom supercomputer was algorithmically unnecessary.
Postman's own log file records the silent auto-installation of Claude Code and Codex plugins with the source field literally labeled 'auto-existing-upgrade,' timestamped to the second.

ETH Zurich's diabetes implant doesn't move glucose into cells — it electrochemically converts excess blood sugar into gluconate, a substance the body simply excretes, removing the energy entirely rather than storing it as fat.

The near-inaudible Doppler curve of aircraft background noise in any video recording can be cross-referenced against ADS-B transponder data to identify the exact geographic location of the person who filmed it.

make_something.prompt: Build a WebGL sketch that listens to microphone input, visualizes the ambient frequency spectrum in real time, and attempts to detect and highlight a simulated 'hidden signal' band — a narrow frequency range that pulses on a slow, near-imperceptible rhythm. Make the detection feel like the sketch is noticing something the viewer isn't. The point isn't the signal itself but the sensation of a system becoming aware of something just below conscious threshold — which is what today's acoustic OSINT piece is actually about.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film structured like a piece of software — memory, ritual, and time as feedback loops, with Tokyo youth culture and Guinea-Bissau funeral rites as the two poles. Marker treats the camera as a tool for thinking, not recording, and the result is the closest cinema has come to feeling like the inside of a mind trying to hold the world together.

art_picks.title: Music for 18 Musicians
art_picks.creator: Steve Reich
art_picks.why: A living system, not a composition — interlocking pulses that gradually phase against each other until the whole room seems to breathe. The score is a machine whose emergent behavior you can feel in your body before you can name it; exactly the kind of deep structure with expressive surface that holds up across decades.

art_picks.title: The Crossing
art_picks.creator: Bill Viola
art_picks.why: Two-channel video of a figure consumed simultaneously by fire and water — elemental, ritual, and physically overwhelming at scale. Viola goes unreasonably deep on the phenomenology of the body as a threshold between inner and outer worlds, and the work earns every second of its duration.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, 11 West 53rd St, Manhattan
events.why: Huyghe worked with neuroscientists to scan a human brain mid-imagination, fed the fMRI data to a neural network, and the hallucinatory output plays on outdoor screens — activated in real time by visitor gaze and cancer cell mutation data; it's a live system that poses the question of what a non-human mind actually sees, and it closes at the end of the month.

events.name: Cristina Iglesias: Possible Matter
events.why: Her first NY show with Hauser & Wirth debuts a new immersive aluminum-and-colored-glass dome alongside sculptures that blur the line between built and natural worlds — the kind of environmental work that makes a space think.

events.name: Hard Art
events.venue: MoMA PS1, 22-25 Jackson Ave, Long Island City
events.why: Opens November 5 with an open-house day — a group show on abstract painting by Black artists that's been flagged as one of the month's most compelling conceptual exhibitions by multiple independent NYC art writers.

events.name: Jason Moran: STACKS
events.why: Jazz pianist Moran makes visual art where the centerpiece is two parlor pianos stacked precariously on top of each other — improvisation as physical precarity, music as object, the kind of category-collapse that earns the trip to Chelsea on its own.

events.name: Art Week NYC — Gallery Openings & New Museum Programming
events.venue: Citywide: Chelsea, Tribeca, LES, UES, and Midtown hub
events.why: 76+ galleries across the city opening simultaneously, with public programming co-hosted by the New Museum and Artforum — less art fair, more concentrated access to the scene at its most activated; the Nov 14 New Museum day is the anchor.
